config.title: Reusable Button

intro.title: Reusable Button
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a reusable button component in Angular. You will learn how to create a custom component that can be used multiple times across your application with different labels and styles. The core concept is component-based architecture, which allows you to encapsulate functionality and UI into a single, reusable piece. You will use TypeScript for the component logic and Angular's template syntax for the structure. By the end, you'll have a flexible button that can be customized through input properties.
intro.usecase: Reusable buttons are foundational components in modern web applications, appearing consistently across interfaces like e-commerce checkout flows, social media platforms, and SaaS dashboards. In Angular applications, you'll implement reusable button components for consistent actions like 'Submit' in forms, 'Add to Cart' in product listings, or 'Filter' in data tables. This pattern allows development teams to maintain visual consistency while enabling product managers to update button behavior globally. By mastering reusable buttons, you'll build more maintainable interfaces where design changes propagate instantly across entire applications.

objectives: Construct a reusable Angular button component with TypeScript
Configure button properties using @Input decorators for customization
Implement event handling with @Output decorators for user interactions
Apply CSS styling to create visually consistent button variants
Initialize and bind component data to control button behavior
Render the reusable button component within parent templates
Manipulate button states and appearances through property binding

steps.title: Import Component and CommonModule from @angular/core
steps.instruction: Import the Component decorator from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with the correct module paths. The Component decorator is needed to define Angular components, and CommonModule provides common directives like *ngIf and *ngFor.
steps.seedCode: // Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for Component and CommonModule are added to the file.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some imports, but make sure to import both Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Create the ButtonComponent class with @Component decorator
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript class named ButtonComponent and apply the @Component decorator with selector: 'app-button' and template: '<button>Click me</button>'
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator from '@angular/core' that you imported in the previous step. The class should be exported.
steps.expectedOutcome: A basic Angular component class is created with proper decorator configuration
successCriteria: ButtonComponent class is defined with @Component decorator containing selector 'app-button' and template with a button element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have: 1) exported class ButtonComponent, 2) @Component decorator with selector 'app-button', and 3) template with a button element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component structure isn't complete. Remember to define a class named ButtonComponent and apply the @Component decorator with the specified selector and template.

steps.title: Add Input property for button text with type annotation
steps.instruction: Inside the ButtonComponent class, add a public property called 'text' with the @Input() decorator and type it as string.
steps.hint: Use @Input() decorator from @angular/core to make the property configurable from parent components.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of an input property in Angular
@Input() label: string;
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonComponent will have a configurable 'text' property that can receive values from parent components.
successCriteria: The ButtonComponent class contains a public property named 'text' decorated with @Input() and typed as string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added the @Input() decorator and typed the property as string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input property is missing or incorrect. Check that you've added '@Input() text: string;' inside the ButtonComponent class.

steps.title: Add Input property for button type with default value
steps.instruction: Add a new Input property called 'type' with a string type and a default value of 'button' in the ButtonComponent class.
steps.hint: Use the @Input decorator with a type annotation and assign a default value directly in the property declaration.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Input property with default value
@Input() color: string = 'blue';
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonComponent will have a 'type' input property that defaults to 'button' when not provided.
successCriteria: The ButtonComponent class contains an @Input() type: string = 'button'; property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a 'type' property, but check that it uses @Input(), has string type, and defaults to 'button'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The 'type' input property is missing or incorrect. Ensure it's decorated with @Input(), typed as string, and defaults to 'button'.

steps.title: Add Input property for button disabled state
steps.instruction: In the ButtonComponent class, add an @Input property named 'disabled' with a boolean type annotation and a default value of false.
steps.hint: Use the same pattern as the 'text' and 'type' properties, but with boolean type and default value false.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: boolean input property
@Input() isActive: boolean = false;
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonComponent will have a boolean 'disabled' input property that can control the button's disabled state.
successCriteria: The ButtonComponent class contains an @Input property named 'disabled' with boolean type and default value false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added an @Input property named 'disabled' with boolean type and default value false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The disabled input property is missing or incorrect. It should be an @Input with boolean type and default value false.

steps.title: Add Output property for click events
steps.instruction: Add an output property called 'onClick' using EventEmitter to emit click events from the ButtonComponent.
steps.hint: Use the @Output decorator and EventEmitter from @angular/core to create an event emitter property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating an output property
@Output() itemSelected = new EventEmitter<string>();
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonComponent will have an output property 'onClick' that can emit events when the button is clicked.
successCriteria: The component has an @Output property named 'onClick' that is an EventEmitter instance.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've used both @Output decorator and EventEmitter for the onClick property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The onClick output property is not properly defined. Remember to use @Output decorator with EventEmitter from @angular/core.

steps.title: Create the button click handler method
steps.instruction: Inside the ButtonComponent class, create a method named handleClick that emits the onClick event when called.
steps.hint: Define a method that calls the emit method on the onClick EventEmitter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ButtonComponent will have a handleClick method that can be called to emit click events.
successCriteria: The ButtonComponent class contains a handleClick method that calls emit() on the onClick EventEmitter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a method, but make sure it's named handleClick and calls emit() on the onClick EventEmitter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleClick method is missing or doesn't properly emit the onClick event. Check the method name and that it calls emit().

steps.title: Build the button template with basic structure
steps.instruction: Add a button element to the component's template property inside the @Component decorator.
steps.hint: The button should be a basic HTML button element. You'll add attributes and event bindings in later steps.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a basic element to a template template: '
Content
'
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now contains a basic button element.
successCriteria: The template property contains a button element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a button element inside the template property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template should contain a button element. Check that you've added it correctly.

steps.title: Bind input properties to button attributes
steps.instruction: In the button element's template, bind the text, type, and disabled input properties to the corresponding button attributes using property binding syntax.
steps.hint: Use square brackets [] for property binding. For example, [disabled]="disabled" binds the disabled input property to the button's disabled attribute.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: binding properties in a template
<button [type]="buttonType" [disabled]="isDisabled">Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button element in the template will have property bindings for text content, type, and disabled state.
successCriteria: The button element includes property bindings for [innerText] or text interpolation, [type], and [disabled] attributes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some property bindings, but make sure all three (text, type, disabled) are properly bound to the button attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element doesn't have the required property bindings. Remember to use [attribute]="property" syntax for each input property.

steps.title: Wire click handler to button click event
steps.instruction: Bind the button's click event to the handleClick method using Angular event binding syntax.
steps.hint: Use parentheses around the event name and assign it to the component method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will trigger the handleClick method when clicked, which emits the onClick event.
successCriteria: The button element has (click)="handleClick()" event binding applied.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using Angular's event binding syntax with parentheses.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button click event isn't properly bound. Check the event binding syntax.
